units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Algebraic expressions
units.caps: CAPS Grade 8 Mathematics, Term 2: Algebraic expressions (like terms; add, subtract, multiply and divide expressions; expand using the distributive law)
units.intention: Today I am simplifying expressions and expanding brackets.
units.prompt: How did you decide which terms were like terms?

lesson.say: Like terms have the same letter and the same exponent. Three x and five x are like terms. Three x and five y are not.
lesson.html:
3x + 5x = 8x→3x + 5y stays

Only add or subtract like terms.

lesson.say: To simplify four a plus three b minus a plus two b, group like terms. Four a minus a is three a. Three b plus two b is five b. The answer is three a plus five b.
lesson.html:
4a − a = 3a→3b + 2b = 5b→3a + 5b

Group, then combine.

lesson.say: To expand three times x plus four in brackets, multiply each term inside by three. Three x plus twelve.
lesson.html:
3(x + 4)→= 3x + 12

The distributive law: multiply every term inside.

steps: Expand: 2x + 10.
Add 3x: 2x + 10 + 3x.
Combine like terms: 5x + 10.

questions.q: Which are like terms?
questions.explain: 7y and −2y have the same variable and exponent.

questions.q: Simplify: 6m + 2n − 4m
questions.explain: 6m − 4m = 2m, so 2m + 2n.

questions.q: Expand: 5(2a − 3)
Expand: x(x + 6)
Simplify: 3(p + 2) − p

units.parent: Your child simplified algebraic expressions and expanded brackets.
units.teacher: Shows identifying like terms, simplifying expressions and applying the distributive law, including with a variable outside the bracket.
units.done: Combine like terms and multiply every term inside the brackets.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: The Theorem of Pythagoras
units.caps: CAPS Grade 8 Mathematics, Term 3: Theorem of Pythagoras (determine whether a triangle is right-angled; calculate missing lengths)
units.intention: Today I am using Pythagoras to find a missing side.
units.prompt: How do you know which side is the hypotenuse?

lesson.say: In a right-angled triangle, the longest side is opposite the right angle. It is called the hypotenuse.
lesson.html: c is the hypotenuse, opposite the square corner.

lesson.say: The square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. So c squared equals a squared plus b squared.
lesson.html:
c² = a² + b²

This only works for right-angled triangles.

lesson.say: If the two shorter sides are three and four, then c squared is nine plus sixteen, which is twenty-five. So c is five.
lesson.html: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25→c = √25 = 5

example.q: A ladder leans against a wall. Its foot is 6 m from the wall and it reaches 8 m up. How long is the ladder?
steps: The wall and ground make a right angle. The ladder is the hypotenuse.

questions.q: The two shorter sides are 5 cm and 12 cm. How long is the hypotenuse?
questions.html: <svg width="170" height="130" viewBox="0 0 170 130" role="img" aria-label="Right-angled triangle with sides 5, 12 and hypotenuse ?"><polygon points="20,110 150,110 20,20" fill="var(--brand-soft)" stroke="var(--ink)" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="20" y="96" width="14" height="14" fill="none" stroke="var(--ink)"/><text x="85" y="126" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--ink)">12</text><text x="8" y="70" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--ink)">5</text><text x="98" y="58" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--ink)">?</text></svg>
questions.explain: c² = 169, so c = 13 cm.

questions.q: Which side is the hypotenuse?
options: The side opposite the right angle
hints: Look across from the square corner.
questions.explain: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle.

questions.q: Is a triangle with sides 6, 8 and 10 right-angled?
questions.explain: 6² + 8² = 100 = 10², so yes.

questions.q: The hypotenuse is 10 and one side is 6. Find the other side.
Is a triangle with sides 4, 5 and 6 right-angled?
questions.explain: 41 ≠ 36, so it is not right-angled.

units.parent: Your child used the Theorem of Pythagoras to find missing sides of right-angled triangles.
units.teacher: Shows identifying the hypotenuse, applying the theorem to find a missing side and testing whether a triangle is right-angled.
units.done: In a right-angled triangle, c² = a² + b².

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Simple and compound interest
units.caps: CAPS Grade 8 Mathematics, Term 1: Financial mathematics (profit, loss, discount, VAT; simple and compound interest; hire purchase)
units.intention: Today I am calculating interest on savings and loans.
units.prompt: Would you rather save with simple or compound interest? Why?

lesson.say: Simple interest is paid only on the amount you start with. R1 000 at ten percent simple interest earns R100 every year.
lesson.html:
Year 1: +R100→Year 2: +R100→Year 3: +R100

Simple interest = principal × rate × time.

lesson.say: Compound interest is paid on the amount plus the interest already earned. R1 000 at ten percent becomes R1 100, then R1 210, then R1 331.
lesson.html:
R1 000→R1 100→R1 210→R1 331

Interest earns interest. It grows faster over time.

lesson.say: When you borrow, interest works against you. Buying on credit or hire purchase can cost much more than the cash price.
lesson.html:
💳 📈

Compare the total cost, not just the monthly payment.

example.q: You invest R2 000 at 5% simple interest for 3 years. How much interest do you earn?
steps: 5% of R2 000 is R100 per year.
For 3 years: 3 × R100.
R300 interest.

questions.q: R500 at 10% simple interest for 2 years. How much interest?
R1 000 at 10% compound interest. How much after 2 years?
Why does compound interest grow faster?
options: You earn interest on your interest
The rate goes up each year
hints: Interest is worked out on the new total.
questions.explain: Each year's interest is added to the amount, so you earn interest on interest.

questions.q: A TV costs R4 000 cash, or R250 a month for 24 months. How much more does credit cost?
What is 15% VAT on R200?

units.parent: Your child calculated simple and compound interest and compared the cost of credit with cash.
units.teacher: Shows calculating simple and compound interest, VAT and the total cost of credit.
units.done: Compound interest grows on itself. Borrowing adds to the cost.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Poem: Morning in Our Street
units.caps: CAPS Grade 8 English Home Language: Literature (poetry: imagery, figures of speech, rhyme, tone and mood)
units.intention: Today I am analysing imagery, tone and mood in a poem.
units.prompt: Which line created the clearest picture for you?
units.passage:
Morning in Our Street (a 2to.iQ poem)

Before the sun has rubbed its eyes,
the taxis hoot their sharp goodbyes;
a rooster shouts from someone's yard,
the pavement, cold and grey and hard.

Mama Thandi lights her stove,
the vetkoek dance in oil and rise;
the smell runs down the street to find
each sleepy child with hungry eyes.

And we, in blue and grey and green,
a river flowing to the school,
are pebbles carried, side by side,
still sleepy, laughing, breaking rules.

lesson.say: Read the poem, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Morning in Our Street (a 2to.iQ poem)

Before the sun has rubbed its eyes,
the taxis hoot their sharp goodbyes;
a rooster shouts from someone's yard,
the pavement, cold and grey and hard.

Mama Thandi lights her stove,
the vetkoek dance in oil and rise;
the smell runs down the street to find
each sleepy child with hungry eyes.

And we, in blue and grey and green,
a river flowing to the school,
are pebbles carried, side by side,
still sleepy, laughing, breaking rules.

lesson.say: Imagery is language that appeals to the senses. The smell runs down the street appeals to smell. The taxis hoot appeals to sound.
lesson.html:
Sight→Sound→Smell→Touch→Taste

Imagery helps us see, hear and smell the street.

lesson.say: Tone is the poet's attitude. Here it is warm and fond. Mood is the feeling the reader gets: cosy, lively and familiar.
lesson.html:
Tone: the writer's attitude→Mood: the reader's feeling

The children as a river and pebbles is an extended metaphor.

example.q: What figure of speech is: Before the sun has rubbed its eyes?
steps: Can the sun rub its eyes?
No, that is a human action.
It is personification, showing it is very early morning.

questions.q: Which sense does the vetkoek dance in oil mostly appeal to?
questions.explain: We picture the vetkoek moving in the oil.

questions.q: What is the tone of the poem?
hints: How does the poet feel about the street?
questions.explain: The poet describes the street with warmth and affection.

questions.q: The children are a river flowing to the school. What does this suggest?
options: They move together in a steady stream
questions.explain: Like a river, the children flow together towards school.

questions.q: Which words rhyme in stanza 1?
questions.explain: Eyes and goodbyes rhyme; yard and hard rhyme.

questions.q: What does in blue and grey and green describe?
questions.explain: The colours describe different school uniforms.

reflect.q: How did you understand the poem best?

units.parent: Your child analysed a poem's imagery, tone, mood and figures of speech.
units.teacher: Shows identifying sensory imagery, personification, extended metaphor, rhyme scheme, tone and mood.
units.done: Imagery, tone and mood bring a poem to life.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Active and passive voice
units.caps: CAPS Grade 8 English Home Language: Language Structures and Conventions (active and passive voice; subject and object; tense)
units.intention: Today I am changing sentences between active and passive voice.
units.prompt: When might a writer choose the passive voice?

lesson.say: In the active voice, the subject does the action. The dog chased the cat. The dog is doing the chasing.
lesson.html:
The dog chased the cat.

Subject → verb → object.

lesson.say: In the passive voice, the object becomes the subject, and the action is done to it. The cat was chased by the dog.
lesson.html:
The cat was chased by the dog.

Passive uses a form of to be plus the past participle.

lesson.say: Keep the same tense. Active: Thandi writes the report. Passive: The report is written by Thandi. Active: She wrote it. Passive: It was written by her.
lesson.html:
writes → is written→wrote → was written→will write → will be written

The passive is useful when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

example.q: Change to passive: The learners planted the trees.
steps: The object is the trees. It becomes the subject.
Planted is past tense, so use were planted.
The trees were planted by the learners.

questions.q: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
options: The window was broken by the ball.
hints: Look for was or were plus a past participle.
The action is done to the subject.
questions.explain: The window was broken by the ball. is passive.

questions.q: Change to passive: The chef cooks the meal.
options: The meal is cooked by the chef.
The meal was cooked by the chef.
The chef is cooked by the meal.
hints: The meal is cooked by the chef.
questions.explain: Present tense active → is cooked.

questions.q: Change to active: The song was sung by the choir.
hints: Was sung is past, so sang.
questions.explain: The choir sang the song.

questions.q: Why might a news report say: The bank was robbed last night?
questions.explain: The passive works when we do not know who did it.

questions.q: Change to passive: They will announce the results.
hints: Use will be plus the past participle.
questions.explain: Future active → will be announced.

units.parent: Your child changed sentences between active and passive voice.
units.teacher: Shows converting between active and passive voice across tenses and explaining when the passive is used.
units.done: Active: the subject acts. Passive: the action is done to the subject.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Persuasive language
units.caps: CAPS Grade 8 English Home Language: Reading and Viewing, Listening and Speaking (persuasive texts and advertisements; emotive language; fact and opinion; bias)
units.intention: Today I am spotting persuasive techniques in adverts and speeches.
units.prompt: Which technique works on you most often?

lesson.say: Emotive words make us feel strongly. Desperate, heroic, shocking. They push us towards a feeling, not just a fact.
lesson.html:
desperate→amazing→shocking→heroic

Emotive language targets feelings.

lesson.say: Advertisers use the bandwagon effect, everyone is buying it. Testimonials from famous people. Statistics. And rhetorical questions, like don't you deserve the best?
lesson.html:
Bandwagon→Testimonial→Statistics→Rhetorical question

Ask: who benefits if I believe this?

lesson.say: A fact can be checked. An opinion is a belief. Bias is when a text only shows one side.
lesson.html:
Fact: can be proven→Opinion: a belief→Bias: one-sided

Good readers question what they read.

example.q: An advert says: 9 out of 10 dentists choose Brite toothpaste! Which technique is this?
steps: It uses a number to sound convincing.
It also uses experts.
Statistics and expert testimonial. Ask: which dentists, and who paid for the survey?

questions.q: Join millions of happy customers! Which technique is this?
hints: It says everyone is doing it.
questions.explain: It suggests everyone is buying it: bandwagon.

questions.q: Which is a fact?
options: This is the best stadium in Africa.
questions.explain: The number of seats can be checked.

questions.q: Why would you want to miss out? What is this?
questions.explain: It is asked to persuade, not for an answer.

questions.q: A report about a mine only interviews the mine owner. What is the problem?
questions.explain: Only one side is shown, so it is biased.

questions.q: Fact or opinion?
items: Water boils at 100 °C at sea level
Cape Town is in the Western Cape
questions.explain: Boiling point and location are facts. Worst and boring are opinions.

reflect.q: Which technique will you watch for?

units.parent: Your child learned to spot persuasive techniques, tell fact from opinion and recognise bias.
units.teacher: Shows identifying persuasive techniques, distinguishing fact from opinion and recognising bias.
units.done: Question persuasive texts: check the facts and look for bias.

units.subject: Natural Sciences
units.title: Photosynthesis and respiration
units.topic: How plants and animals use energy
units.caps: CAPS Grade 8 Natural Sciences, Term 1 Life and Living: Photosynthesis and respiration (word equations; the role of light, carbon dioxide, water, glucose and oxygen)
units.intention: Today I am comparing photosynthesis and respiration.
units.prompt: Why do animals depend on plants?

lesson.say: Plants make food by photosynthesis. Carbon dioxide plus water, with light energy, makes glucose and oxygen.
lesson.html:
carbon dioxide + water→→ light →→glucose + oxygen

It happens in chloroplasts, which contain green chlorophyll.

lesson.say: All living things release energy from food by respiration. Glucose plus oxygen makes carbon dioxide, water and energy.
lesson.html:
glucose + oxygen→→→carbon dioxide + water + energy

Respiration happens in every living cell, day and night.

lesson.say: Photosynthesis and respiration are opposites. Plants give out oxygen that animals breathe in. Animals give out carbon dioxide that plants use.
lesson.html:
🌿 ⇄ 🐄

They keep oxygen and carbon dioxide in balance.

steps: Respiration happens in all living cells.
It does not need light.
Yes, plants respire day and night. They only photosynthesise in light.

questions.q: What do plants need for photosynthesis?
hints: Look at the left side of the equation.
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide, water and light energy.

questions.q: What gas do plants release during photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Plants release oxygen.

questions.q: What is the purpose of respiration?
hints: What do cells need to work?
questions.explain: Respiration releases energy from glucose.

questions.q: Where in the plant cell does photosynthesis happen?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts.

questions.q: Which process uses each?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis uses light and makes glucose. Respiration uses glucose and releases energy.

units.parent: Your child compared photosynthesis and respiration using word equations.
units.teacher: Shows writing word equations for photosynthesis and respiration and explaining their interdependence.
units.done: Plants make food by photosynthesis. All living things release energy by respiration.

units.subject: Natural Sciences
units.title: Atoms, elements and compounds
units.caps: CAPS Grade 8 Natural Sciences, Term 2 Matter and Materials: Atoms (structure of the atom; elements and the Periodic Table; compounds; the particle model)
units.intention: Today I am learning what atoms are and how they make elements and compounds.
units.prompt: How can just over 100 elements make everything around us?

lesson.say: Everything is made of atoms. An atom has a nucleus with protons and neutrons, and electrons moving around it.
lesson.html:
⚛️

Protons +→Neutrons 0→Electrons −

Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.

lesson.say: An element is made of only one kind of atom. Oxygen, iron and carbon are elements. They are listed on the Periodic Table with symbols, like O, Fe and C.
lesson.html:
O oxygen→Fe iron→C carbon→Na sodium

There are 118 known elements.

lesson.say: A compound forms when two or more elements join chemically. Water is H two O: two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
lesson.html:
H₂O water→CO₂ carbon dioxide→NaCl table salt

A compound has new properties, different from its elements.

example.q: Is table salt, NaCl, an element or a compound?
steps: Look at the symbols: Na and Cl.
There are two different elements, joined.
It is a compound.

questions.q: What is in the nucleus of an atom?
questions.explain: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons.

questions.q: Which is an element?
questions.explain: Iron is made of only iron atoms.

questions.q: How many atoms are in one molecule of H₂O?
questions.explain: Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom: 3.

questions.q: What charge does an electron have?
questions.explain: Electrons have a negative charge.

questions.q: Element or compound?
hints: O₂ and Au have one kind.
CO₂ and H₂O have two kinds.
questions.explain: O₂ and Au are elements. CO₂ and H₂O are compounds.

units.parent: Your child learned about atoms and how elements combine to make compounds.
units.teacher: Shows knowledge of subatomic particles, chemical symbols and distinguishing elements from compounds.
units.done: Atoms make elements. Elements join to make compounds.

units.subject: Natural Sciences
units.title: Electric circuits
units.caps: CAPS Grade 8 Natural Sciences, Term 3 Energy and Change: Energy transfer in electrical systems (components of circuits; series and parallel; effects of current; circuit diagrams)
units.intention: Today I am learning how electric circuits work.
units.prompt: Why are the lights in a house wired in parallel?

lesson.say: Electricity only flows in a complete, closed loop. A circuit needs three things. It needs a source of energy, such as a cell. It needs conductors, such as wires. And it needs a device, such as a bulb.
lesson.html:
Cell→Wire→Switch→Bulb→Wire

Open the switch and the loop is broken.

lesson.say: In a series circuit, components are in one loop. If one bulb breaks, all the bulbs go out. More bulbs in series make each bulb dimmer.
lesson.html:
🔋 → 💡 → 💡 ↩

Series: one path.

lesson.say: In a parallel circuit, each component has its own branch. If one bulb breaks, the others stay on.
lesson.html:
🔋 ⇉ 💡 💡

Parallel: several paths. Houses are wired in parallel.

example.q: Two bulbs are in series. One blows. What happens?
steps: Series has only one path.
A blown bulb breaks the loop.
Both bulbs go out.

questions.q: What does a switch do?
hints: It breaks or completes the loop.
questions.explain: A switch opens or closes the circuit.

questions.q: Which material is a good conductor?
questions.explain: Copper conducts electricity well.

questions.q: In a parallel circuit, one bulb blows. What happens to the others?
hints: Each bulb has its own path.
The other paths are still complete.
questions.explain: Other branches remain complete, so the bulbs stay on.

questions.q: What happens when you add more bulbs in series?
hints: The energy is shared along one path.
questions.explain: Bulbs in series share the energy, so each is dimmer.

questions.q: Why is it dangerous to touch a plug with wet hands?
questions.explain: Water can conduct electricity through your body.

units.parent: Your child learned about complete circuits, series and parallel circuits, and electrical safety.
units.teacher: Shows understanding of circuit components, comparing series and parallel circuits, conductors and safety.
units.done: Electricity needs a complete circuit. Parallel circuits keep other branches working.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Career fields
units.caps: CAPS Grade 8 Life Orientation: World of work (career fields; interests and abilities; subject choices for Grade 10; sources of career information)
units.intention: Today I am matching my interests to career fields.
units.prompt: Which career field fits you, and why?

lesson.say: Careers can be grouped into fields. Some fields are health, engineering and building, and business. Others are arts and design, agriculture, education and information technology.
lesson.html:
Health→Engineering→Business→Arts→Agriculture→IT

Each field has jobs at different levels of study.

lesson.say: Think about what you enjoy and what you are good at. Do you like working with people, with your hands, with ideas or with data?
lesson.html:
People→Things→Ideas→Data

Match interests and abilities to fields.

lesson.say: There are many paths: university, a TVET college, a learnership or apprenticeship, or starting a business. Grade 9 subject choices can open or close some paths, so find out early.
lesson.html:
University→TVET college→Learnership→Own business

Ask: what subjects does this career need?

example.q: Ayanda loves fixing bikes and is good at Technology. Which field could suit her?
steps: She likes working with her hands and things.
She is strong in Technology.
Engineering and building, such as a mechanic or technician, could suit her.

questions.q: Which career is in the health field?
questions.explain: Nursing is in the health field.

questions.q: Someone who loves organising data and numbers might enjoy …
questions.explain: Accounting and data analysis work with numbers and data.

questions.q: Which is a path to a trade like plumbing?
hints: Trades are learned by doing the work.
questions.explain: Trades are usually learned at TVET colleges and through apprenticeships.

questions.q: Why are Grade 9 subject choices important?
options: They can open or close some career paths
questions.explain: Some careers need specific Grade 10 to 12 subjects.

questions.q: Match interest to field.
questions.explain: Caring for the sick and dentistry are health. Logos and murals are arts and design.

reflect.q: Which way of working do you enjoy most?

units.parent: Your child explored career fields and how interests and subject choices link to careers. Talk together about what they enjoy.
units.teacher: Shows knowledge of career fields, matching interests and abilities, and awareness of study pathways.
units.done: Match your interests and abilities to career fields, and check which subjects you need.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Making safe decisions
units.caps: CAPS Grade 8 Life Orientation: Health, social and environmental responsibility (risky behaviour and situations; decision-making steps; where to get help)
units.intention: Today I am using steps to make safe decisions.
units.prompt: Who could you go to for help with a hard decision?

lesson.say: A risky situation could lead to harm. Examples are being alone with someone you do not trust, or meeting an online stranger. Getting into a car with a driver who has been drinking is also risky.
lesson.html:
⚠️

Trust your gut feeling. If something feels wrong, it may be.

lesson.say: Use these steps. Stop. Think about the choices. Think about the consequences for you and others. Choose the safest option. Then reflect.
lesson.html:
Stop→Options→Consequences→Choose→Reflect

Taking a moment helps you avoid pressure.

lesson.say: You do not have to decide alone. Talk to a trusted adult, a teacher or a counsellor. Childline South Africa is free on 116.
lesson.html:
Trusted adult→Teacher→Counsellor→Childline 116

Asking for help is a strength.

example.q: After a party, a friend's older brother offers Sizwe a lift, but he has been drinking. What should Sizwe do?
steps: Stop: this is risky.
Options: accept, phone a parent, or get a lift with a sober adult.
Choose: phone a parent or another trusted adult. His safety comes first.

questions.q: What is the first step in making a safe decision?
questions.explain: Stopping gives you time to think.

questions.q: Someone you met online asks to meet you alone. What is safest?
options: Tell a trusted adult and do not go alone
hints: You do not really know this person.
questions.explain: Tell a trusted adult. Never meet an online stranger alone.

questions.q: What is the free number for Childline South Africa?
questions.explain: Childline South Africa is 116, free.

questions.q: Why think about consequences?
options: To see how a choice affects you and others
questions.explain: Consequences show how a choice affects you and others.

questions.q: Put the decision steps in order.
hints: Then think of choices and their results.
questions.explain: Stop, options, consequences, choose, reflect.

reflect.q: Which step is hardest for you?

units.parent: Your child practised decision-making steps and learned where to get help, including Childline on 116.
units.teacher: Shows recognising risky situations, applying a decision-making model and identifying support services.
units.done: Stop, think, choose the safest option, and ask for help.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Diversity and prejudice
units.caps: CAPS Grade 8 Life Orientation: Constitutional rights and responsibilities; Social and environmental responsibility (cultural diversity; stereotyping, prejudice and discrimination; respect)
units.intention: Today I am learning how stereotypes and prejudice affect people.
units.prompt: How can you include someone who is different from you?

lesson.say: South Africa has 12 official languages and many cultures and beliefs. Diversity means a mix of different people. It makes communities richer.
lesson.html:
🌍 🤝

South Africa is often called the Rainbow Nation.

lesson.say: A stereotype is a fixed idea about a whole group, like saying all boys are bad at cooking. Prejudice is judging someone before you know them.
lesson.html:
Stereotype: a fixed idea→Prejudice: judging early→Discrimination: unfair treatment

Stereotypes ignore that every person is an individual.

lesson.say: You can challenge a stereotype by asking, is that true for everyone? You can include people, and report unfair treatment.
lesson.html:
Question it→Include others→Report it

The Constitution protects everyone from unfair discrimination.

example.q: A classmate says: Girls can't be engineers. How could you respond?
steps: Notice it is a stereotype about a whole group.
Ask: is that true for every girl?
Share an example: many South African women are engineers.

questions.q: How many official languages does South Africa have?
hints: South African Sign Language became official in 2023.
questions.explain: South Africa has 12 official languages, including South African Sign Language.

questions.q: Which is a stereotype?
options: All old people are bad with phones
hints: A fixed idea about a whole group.
questions.explain: It judges a whole group.

questions.q: What is discrimination?
options: Treating someone unfairly because of their group
questions.explain: Discrimination is unfair treatment because of who someone is.

questions.q: Which is a good way to challenge a stereotype?
options: Ask if it is true for everyone
hints: Ask if it is true for everyone.
questions.explain: Questioning it helps people think again.

questions.q: Inclusive or exclusive?
items: Inviting a new learner to sit with you
Learning a greeting in a classmate's language
Leaving someone out because of their religion
questions.explain: Inviting and learning a greeting are inclusive.

units.parent: Your child explored diversity, stereotypes, prejudice and ways to be inclusive.
units.teacher: Shows distinguishing stereotype, prejudice and discrimination, and strategies to challenge them.
units.done: Every person is an individual. Question stereotypes and include others.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Solving linear equations
units.caps: Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics (0862), Stage 8: Algebra (solving linear equations, including with brackets and unknowns on both sides)
units.intention: Today I am solving equations with unknowns on both sides.
units.prompt: How is an equation like a balance scale?

lesson.say: An equation is like a balance. Whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other.
lesson.html: Do the same to both sides.

lesson.say: Expand brackets first. 3 times x plus 2 equals 21 becomes 3x plus 6 equals 21. Then 3x equals 15, so x equals 5.
Collect the x terms on one side. 5x plus 3 equals 2x plus 12. Subtract 2x: 3x plus 3 equals 12. So 3x equals 9 and x equals 3.

steps: Subtract 2x from both sides: 2x − 7 = 5.
Divide by 2: x = 6.

questions.q: Solve 2x + 5 = 17.
Solve 4(x − 1) = 20.
Solve 7x + 2 = 3x + 18.
Solve x ÷ 3 = 9.
Check: is x = 5 a solution of 3x − 4 = 11?

options: Doing the same to both sides

units.parent: Your child solved equations with brackets and unknowns on both sides.
units.teacher: Shows solving linear equations involving brackets and unknowns on both sides, and verifying solutions.
units.done: Expand, collect the unknowns on one side, solve, then check.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Percentage increase and decrease
units.caps: Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics (0862), Stage 8: Number (percentage increase and decrease; using multipliers)
units.intention: Today I am working out percentage increases and decreases.
units.prompt: How do you know if a sale is really a bargain?

lesson.say: To find 20 percent of 50, divide by 100 and multiply by 20, or multiply by 0.2. 20 percent of 50 is 10.
To increase by 20 percent, multiply by 1.2. To decrease by 20 percent, multiply by 0.8.
lesson.html: +20%: × 1.2→−20%: × 0.8

lesson.say: Percentage change is the change divided by the original amount, times 100. A price rising from 40 to 50 dollars is a 25 percent increase.

example.q: A $60 jacket is reduced by 15%. What is the new price?
steps: Multiplier for a 15% decrease: 0.85.

questions.q: Find 30% of 80.
Which multiplier increases an amount by 5%?
A $200 bike is reduced by 25%. What is the new price, in dollars?
A price rises from $40 to $46. What is the percentage increase? (Type the number only.)
A price goes up 10%, then down 10%. Is it back to the original?
questions.explain: 1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99, so it ends 1% lower.

units.parent: Your child worked out percentage increases, decreases and changes.
units.teacher: Shows calculating percentages of amounts, using multipliers for increase and decrease, and finding percentage change.
units.done: Use a multiplier, and for change: (new − old) ÷ old × 100.

units.subject: English
units.title: Character and setting
units.caps: Cambridge Lower Secondary English (1111), Stage 8: Reading (how writers present character and setting through language and detail)
units.intention: Today I am analysing how a writer reveals a character.
units.prompt: How can you tell someone is worried without them saying so?
units.passage:
The Harbour at Dawn (a 2to.iQ story extract)

The fishing boats came in one by one, low in the water. Uncle Sizwe stood on the wall with his arms folded, counting them the way other men count money. When the last boat rounded the point, his shoulders dropped. He laughed then, too loudly, and clapped the nearest stranger on the back.

lesson.say: Read the text, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
The Harbour at Dawn (a 2to.iQ story extract)

The fishing boats came in one by one, low in the water. Uncle Sizwe stood on the wall with his arms folded, counting them the way other men count money. When the last boat rounded the point, his shoulders dropped. He laughed then, too loudly, and clapped the nearest stranger on the back.

lesson.say: Writers reveal character through what people do, not only what they say. Uncle Sizwe counts the boats and his shoulders drop when the last one returns.
lesson.html: Action→Body language→What it reveals

lesson.say: The harbour at dawn, with boats low in the water, creates a quiet, tense mood. Setting can reflect how characters feel.
lesson.html: Setting shapes mood.

steps: Dropping shoulders show tension leaving the body.
It happens when the last boat returns.
He had been worried, and now he is relieved.

questions.q: Why does Uncle Sizwe count the boats?
options: He is worried that one might not return
hints: Relief when the last one arrives.
questions.explain: He is anxious until every boat is safely back.

questions.q: What does 'the way other men count money' suggest?
options: The boats are as precious to him as money
questions.explain: The comparison shows how much the boats matter.

questions.q: Why does he laugh 'too loudly'?
options: His relief bursts out after the tension
questions.explain: The loud laugh releases his built-up worry.

questions.q: What mood does the setting create at the start?
hints: Dawn, boats low in the water.
questions.explain: The quiet harbour and waiting create tension.

questions.q: Which is the best analysis?
options: The writer shows Uncle Sizwe's worry through his folded arms and careful counting.
questions.explain: It links details to what they reveal.

units.parent: Your child analysed how a writer reveals a character's feelings through actions and setting.
units.teacher: Shows analysing characterisation through action and body language and the effect of setting on mood.
units.done: Actions reveal feelings; setting creates mood.

units.subject: English
units.title: A balanced argument
units.caps: Cambridge Lower Secondary English (1111), Stage 8: Reading and writing (balanced, discursive texts; presenting both sides; reaching a conclusion)
units.intention: Today I am reading and planning a balanced argument.
units.prompt: Is it ever hard to decide which side you're on?
units.passage:
Should our town ban plastic bags? (a 2to.iQ article)

Plastic bags are cheap, light and useful, which is exactly the problem: we use them for minutes and throw them away. In our town, volunteers removed more than 3 000 bags from the river last year.

However, a ban is not simple. Some small shop owners say paper bags cost them five times as much, and some families reuse plastic bags as bin liners.

A charge for each bag may be a fairer first step. Where shops have charged for bags, many shoppers have switched to bags they can reuse.

lesson.say: Read the text, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Should our town ban plastic bags? (a 2to.iQ article)

Plastic bags are cheap, light and useful, which is exactly the problem: we use them for minutes and throw them away. In our town, volunteers removed more than 3 000 bags from the river last year.

However, a ban is not simple. Some small shop owners say paper bags cost them five times as much, and some families reuse plastic bags as bin liners.

A charge for each bag may be a fairer first step. Where shops have charged for bags, many shoppers have switched to bags they can reuse.

lesson.say: A balanced argument presents both sides fairly before reaching a conclusion. This article gives reasons for a ban, then reasons against.
lesson.html: For→Against→Conclusion

lesson.say: Writers use signal words to move between sides: however, on the other hand, despite this. The conclusion weighs the evidence.
lesson.html: However, on the other hand, despite this

example.q: What does the writer conclude, and why?
steps: The writer suggests a charge for each bag.
This avoids the problems of a full ban.
It still encourages reusable bags, as other places have shown.

questions.q: Which is an argument FOR a ban?
options: Volunteers removed over 3 000 bags from the river
Families reuse bags as bin liners
questions.explain: The river pollution supports a ban.

questions.q: Which is an argument AGAINST a ban?
options: Paper bags cost small shops five times as much
hints: Who would be harmed by a ban?
questions.explain: The cost to small shops argues against a ban.

questions.q: Which word signals the move to the other side?
hints: Look at the start of paragraph 2.
questions.explain: 'However' introduces the opposing view.

questions.q: What is the writer's conclusion?
options: A charge for each bag may be a fairer first step
questions.explain: The writer suggests charging for bags.

questions.q: What makes the argument balanced?
options: It fairly presents both sides before concluding
questions.explain: It gives both sides fairly.

units.parent: Your child explored how a balanced argument presents both sides.
units.teacher: Shows identifying arguments for and against, recognising discursive signal words and evaluating a reasoned conclusion.
units.done: Present both sides fairly, signal the switch, and weigh them in the conclusion.

units.subject: Science
units.title: The digestive system
units.caps: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science (0893), Stage 8: Biology (the human digestive system; the role of enzymes; absorption)
units.intention: Today I am following food through the digestive system.
units.prompt: What happens to your lunch after you swallow it?

lesson.say: Food travels from the mouth, down the oesophagus, to the stomach, then the small intestine and the large intestine.
lesson.html: Mouth→Oesophagus→Stomach→Small intestine→Large intestine

lesson.say: Teeth break food into smaller pieces. Enzymes break large molecules into small ones the body can absorb. The stomach's acid helps enzymes there and kills bacteria.
lesson.html: Physical: teeth. Chemical: enzymes.

lesson.say: Small food molecules pass through the wall of the small intestine into the blood. The large intestine absorbs water.
lesson.html: Small intestine: nutrients into the blood→Large intestine: water

example.q: Why must large food molecules be broken down?
steps: Large molecules are too big to pass through the gut wall.
Enzymes break them into small, soluble molecules.
These can be absorbed into the blood.

questions.q: Where does food go after the mouth?
questions.explain: Food is swallowed down the oesophagus.

questions.q: Where are most nutrients absorbed into the blood?
questions.explain: Most absorption happens in the small intestine.

questions.q: What do digestive enzymes do?
options: Break large molecules into small ones
questions.explain: Enzymes break large molecules into smaller ones.

questions.q: What is the main job of the large intestine?
hints: Near the end of the gut.
questions.explain: The large intestine absorbs water.

questions.q: Why does the stomach contain acid?
options: It kills bacteria and helps stomach enzymes work
questions.explain: Acid kills bacteria and provides the right pH for stomach enzymes.

units.parent: Your child followed food through the digestive system.
units.teacher: Shows describing the pathway of digestion, the role of enzymes and acid, and the sites of absorption.
units.done: Teeth and enzymes break food down; the small intestine absorbs it.

units.subject: Science
units.title: Reflection and refraction
units.caps: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science (0893), Stage 8: Physics (reflection and the law of reflection; refraction of light)
units.intention: Today I am explaining how light reflects and bends.
units.prompt: Why does a straw look bent in a glass of water?

lesson.say: Light travels in straight lines called rays. We see objects when light from them enters our eyes.
lesson.html: Light → object → eye

lesson.say: When light hits a mirror, it reflects. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Both angles are measured from the normal. The normal is a line at right angles to the mirror.
lesson.html: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection

lesson.say: Light changes speed when it moves from one material to another, for example from water into air. This makes it change direction, or refract. That is why a straw looks bent.
lesson.html: Change of speed → change of direction

example.q: A ray hits a mirror at 35° to the normal. What is the angle of reflection?
steps: The angle of incidence is 35°.
The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

questions.q: The angle of incidence is 50°. What is the angle of reflection, in degrees?
questions.explain: The angles are equal: 50°.

questions.q: What is the normal?
options: A line at right angles to the surface
questions.explain: The normal is perpendicular to the surface.

questions.q: Why does a straw look bent in water?
options: Light refracts as it passes from water into air
questions.explain: Light changes direction as it leaves the water.

questions.q: What causes refraction?
questions.explain: Changing speed causes a change in direction.

questions.q: How do we see a book on a table?
options: Light reflected from the book enters our eyes
The book makes its own light
questions.explain: Light from a source reflects off the book into our eyes.

units.parent: Your child explained how light reflects off mirrors and bends in water.
units.teacher: Shows applying the law of reflection with reference to the normal and explaining refraction in terms of change of speed.
units.done: Reflection: angles equal. Refraction: speed changes, so direction changes.
